conventions.convention: N ≥ 1; input coordinates are 1-based and query addresses are 0-based. The XOR query at address j reads x_{j+1}; no controlled-oracle access is implicit.
The promise consists exactly of the all-zero input and singleton inputs. Bounded-error correctness is required on every promised input; candidate verification costs a separate query.

Finite adaptive protocols have input-independent nonoracle operations and finite outcome sets. Their coherent realization uses exactly T ordinary XOR queries without asserting uniform generation or bounded gate cost.
The address projectors include identities on response and work and sum to identity. With an explicitly adjoined skip address, the search-address sum is only at most identity.
Padding uses a power of two M with N ≤ M < 2N, assigns zero to invalid addresses, and restores added scratch registers after each simulated query.

The Grover schedule assumes one mark only as a schedule parameter, maximizes an exact rational recurrence over 0 ≤ k ≤ ceil(sqrt(M)), and verifies the measured candidate. Exact preparation, reflection, and classical preprocessing costs are separate from query cost.

load_bearing.statement: A finite-branch algorithm using at most T ordinary Boolean XOR queries on every branch has a finite pure-state unitary realization with exactly T ordinary queries and the same output distribution, without controlled-oracle access.
For the coherent T-query realization, ||ψ_T^i − ψ_T^0|| ≤ 2 sum_{t=0}^{T−1} sqrt(q_{t,i}), where q_{t,i} = ||Π_{i−1} ψ_t^0||².
For every T ≥ 0 query algorithm on N addresses, with final states and query magnitudes as in the cumulative hybrid bound, sum_{i=1}^N ||ψ_T^i − ψ_T^0||² ≤ 4T².

For N ≥ 1 and M = 2^m with N ≤ M < 2N, the zero-completion procedure implements exactly one zero-completed XOR query per raw N-address query, restores all scratch registers, and uses no controlled oracle call.
Every bounded-error decision algorithm and every bounded-error finder for P_N uses at least sqrt(N)/24 standard bit queries. Decision satisfies the stronger bound T ≥ sqrt(N)/12.

On every promised input the fixed-one procedure returns the correct decision and, on a one-marked input, its marked coordinate with probability at least 1−1/M. For N=1 it succeeds with certainty; on the zero input verification always returns no.
For every N ≥ 1, the fixed-one search procedure uses at most 3 sqrt(2N) standard bit queries, including final verification. Nonoracle costs are separate; no polynomial-time claim is made.

published_dependencies.used_for: Finite orthonormal basis completion in the coherent instrument dilation.
The adjoint identity in the Kraus-isometry calculation.
Identifying q with cos(2θ) and converting the Chebyshev recurrence into Grover success probabilities.
Deriving the cosine recurrence together with the addition formula.

concerns.concern: The Statement permits a general 'common final two-outcome measurement', but F1 and proof step 1.1 assume its acceptance operator is a diagonal orthogonal projection. The cited acceptance-probability definition supplies that representation for computational-basis acceptance events, not arbitrary two-outcome POVMs. The claim remains true: for a general acceptance effect 0 ≤ E ≤ I, contractivity gives the same step-2.1 estimate. The proof needs this elementary extension or an explicit measurement-dilation justification.

seams_checked.note: The exact success law, integer-rounding range, one-query iterate cost, and exact gate-access qualifications match their uses. The fixed-one schedule is applied only to singleton inputs in the success analysis.

Uses preserve hidden-instance independence, finite adaptive branching, per-instance 2/3 correctness, and worst-case branch query cost. Query complexity is kept separate from gate and preprocessing costs.

The standard bit-query interface is invoked directly on dyadic registers and explicitly extended by the same XOR basis action to N-level registers. Neither phase kickback nor padding assumes controlled-oracle access.
Dirac outer products respect the root first-argument-linear convention. The counterexample uses the Hermitian trace-zero positive/negative-parts identity with the correct factor of two.
Uses preserve ordered orthonormal computational bases, positive-dimensional registers, big-endian indexing, and the one-dimensional zero-qubit register at N=1.

The cited acceptance definition does supply a diagonal projection for its computational-basis event. The acceptance-gap lemma's extension to arbitrary measurements needs the justification recorded in concerns. No uniform-generation claim is inferred for the coherent realization or upper-bound preprocessing.
